before.descent_text: Standard descent is down the West Ridge, not back down the South Face. From the summit, downclimb/scramble a few hundred feet toward a notch on the ridge, then begin rappelling. Multiple trip reports of this exact route confirm it as a sustained multi-rappel descent through a gully/notch system with no bolts; the stations are fixed pins, nuts and cord of variable quality, slung horns, or anchors built from gear (nuts, small-to-medium cams), so carry a rack sufficient for both the climb and for leaving/building rappel anchors, plus some cord or rap tat. One detailed trip report of this route logged 7 double-rope rappels down the West Ridge line back to the Terror Glacier, building a fresh natural anchor at each station; a separate party descending the same general line but counting differently (single 70m rope, more, shorter pitches) reported roughly 5 rappels down the upper West Ridge to a notch followed by about 9 more rappels down through the gully/South Face terrain to the glacier, with several rappels traversing hard to one side to reach the next station and the final rappel using nearly the full rope length to reach a flat spot on the ice. Two ropes give the fewest rappels. The two-rope stations sit roughly 60 m apart and a single 70 m rope doubled reaches only about 35 m, so on one rope expect roughly twice as many stations: about 14 rappels of 30-35 m, which is what the single-rope party above ended up doing. Expect loose rock in the gully and real risk of the rope hanging up on the traversing raps, so back up rappels and check pulls carefully. The descent ends back on the Terror Glacier at the base of the West Ridge/South Face, from which you re-cross the icefall (same crevasse hazard as the approach, now on tired legs and possibly softer afternoon snow) to regain camp, then reverse the Terror Basin boot path and Goodell Creek Trail to the trailhead.

rappel_detail.pull: Loose blocks sit on this line; clear what you safely can rather than pulling ropes down onto it.
rappel_detail.notes: First rappel off the West Ridge below the notch; stations are fixed pins, nuts and cord of variable quality, or built from gear.
rappel_detail.anchor: gear anchor (nuts/small-med cams, occasional slung horn)
hazards: accounts differ on how much fixed material is in place - some describe stations roughly a rope length apart on fixed pins, nuts and cord, reported replaced in mid-2024, while others describe building every anchor from gear. Carry cord and a rack for anchors either way.
rappel_detail.station: The descent is the West Ridge, not the South Face. The stations are on the skier's-left / west side of the summit; descend the ridge crest from there toward the base of the headwall.

rappel_detail.notes: Continuing down the West Ridge rappel line toward the Terror Glacier.
rappel_detail.station: A large horn anchor, reached by scrambling down the ridge crest.

rappel_detail.notes: Fixed three-pin station; check and back up the cord.
hazards: free-hanging off the overhang, with the next station offset rather than straight below
rappel_detail.station: A three-pin anchor at the start of the ridge; the rappel from it goes down and climber's right off a large overhang.

rappel_detail.notes: Mid-line rappel down steep West Ridge terrain.
rappel_detail.station: Around here the line reaches the notch of the West Ridge gully and switches onto the South Face - one party counted about three and a half double-rope rappels down the ridge to just above that notch, then four more down the face.

rappel_detail.notes: Continuing the descent; two ropes used doubled/joined for close to full-length rappels.
Second-to-last rappel before reaching glacier-adjacent terrain.
Final rappel reaching the Terror Glacier; unrope and walk off from here.
rappel_detail.anchor: fixed anchor (two pins and a nut)
hazards: rockfall onto the base of the route, which is where stashed packs sit
rappel_detail.station: The final rappel is short - about 100 ft by one party's estimate - off a slab anchor of two pins and a nut, landing back on the Terror Glacier above the bergschrund. On the South Face variant it returns you to the base of the route itself, so gear can be left there.

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek to the Glee Peak saddle camp, then through the Terror Glacier icefall to the buttress at the lower-left corner of the face
approach_variants.notes: Park at the small pullout just before Goodell Creek Campground at about 600 ft and pick up the Goodell Creek Trail heading north from the Highway 20 corridor. The first 3.75-4 miles follow an old, gently graded forest roadbed along Goodell Creek, brushy with some downed logs in the first mile, and crossing TWO BOULDER-STREWN WASHOUT SECTIONS where the tread disappears into the creek's flood debris and you pick a line across large boulders. That is the trickiest route-finding of the lower approach. ABOUT 200 YARDS PAST THE SECOND WASHOUT, AT AN OBVIOUS CAMPSITE WITH A FIRE RING, an unsigned climbers' boot path breaks right off the roadbed, historically marked by a stone arrow on the ground at roughly 1,700 ft. That is the turn for Terror Basin; missing it means continuing pointlessly up the McMillan Spire approach. From the turnoff the boot path climbs steeply and directly through forest, hand-over-hand in places on roots and branches, and breaks out of the trees around 5,000-5,200 ft. Above treeline a rising traverse across meadow, slab and early-season snow reaches a saddle or notch at about 6,200 ft near Glee Peak; the standard camp sits about 400 ft below the saddle at roughly 5,800 ft. A seasonal trickle down a rock outcrop a few hundred feet below camp is the early-season water source; by late summer parties melt snow.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; the first ascent was made in mid-June in a low-snow year
hazards: Two boulder-strewn washouts where the tread vanishes, the lower approach's route-finding crux
A broken Terror Glacier icefall with open crevasses that worsens through the season
A camp water source that dries out by late summer
A sustained multi-rappel descent down the West Ridge with no fixed or bolted stations anywhere on the peak
Loose rock in the descent gully and real risk of the rope hanging up on traversing rappels
approach_variants.baseFinding:
AIM FOR THE LOWER-LEFT CORNER OF THE SOUTH FACE WHERE A SMALL ROCK BUTTRESS MEETS THE GLACIER. THAT BUTTRESS IS THE START OF THE ROUTE. It is a place where rock touches ice directly, with no intervening gully, and that is what tells it apart from the peak's other lines.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE WEST RIDGE, WHICH LEAVES THE SAME GLACIER: the West Ridge leaves at a BERGSCHRUND BELOW THE WEST END of the peak and then climbs ABOUT 300 FT OF GULLY before any ridge. If there is a gully above you, you have gone past this route's corner and are set up for the West Ridge.

GETTING THERE IS THE ICEFALL PROBLEM, NOT A NAVIGATION ONE: from camp, rope up and cross the Terror Glacier. THE ICEFALL IN ITS MIDDLE IS BROKEN AND OFTEN HAS OPEN CREVASSES; parties commonly work a LEFT-TRENDING SNOW RAMP OR ICE BRIDGE ABOVE A LARGE CREVASSE to get through it onto gentler slopes beyond. That crossing gets more serious as the season progresses.

SO THE HANDRAIL THROUGH THE ICEFALL IS THE LARGE CREVASSE ITSELF: the way through is above it, trending left. If you are dropping below the big crevasse looking for a bridge, you are on the wrong side of the feature parties use.

A COUNTABLE APPROACH MARKER LOWER DOWN THAT SAVES THE WHOLE DAY: TWO WASHOUTS, then 200 yards, then a fire ring. That is how you find the turn in poor light. A stone arrow may or may not still be there; the second washout and the fire ring are ground features that do not move.
